newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN boss calls Swiss row with Jews a PR disaster.
newsitem.headline: UN boss calls Swiss row with Jews a PR disaster.

text.p: The new U.N. chief Kofi Annan on Thursday called Switzerland's dispute with Jews over the fate of unclaimed bank accounts a public relations disaster and urged an equitable settlement.

"I think the whole issue has been a difficult one for Switzerland and a public relations disaster," he said at a news conference, asked if Switzerland's perceived neutrality as host to U.N. European headquarters had been compromised by the row.
"It's unfortunate it has dragged on for so long," said the Secretary-General on his first visit to Geneva as the United Nations boss.
"I hope the issue will be resolved quickly and appropriately and equitably to the satisfaction of all parties concerned," said Annan, 58, who is from Ghana.
Annan said the world body had no intention of moving its European headquarters in Geneva, Palais des Nations, elsewhere because of the controversy.
"But as far as the United Nations is concerned, I think our agencies will continue to do their work and we have no intention of moving elsewhere."
The dispute has triggered a fierce debate in Swiss society about latent anti-Semitism and caused international uproar.
Jewish groups argue that Switzerland profited blatantly from millions of dollars in unclaimed bank accounts of Holocaust victims and are seeking compensation.

The simmering crisis on Monday claimed the head of the Swiss ambassador to the United States, who resigned after a secret document he wrote calling for "waging war" against Jewish groups and other critics was leaked to the press and triggered uproar.

On Wednesday, New York city and state warned Switzerland that they would make it difficult for Swiss banks to do business in New York unless the Swiss created a fund to compensate victims of Holocaust, the Nazi drive to eliminate the Jews.
Swiss banks say they are already working fast to set up a Holocaust memorial fund and urged New York politicians to study the facts before deciding on a threatened boycott.
Bank spokesmen said they took the boycott threat seriously but were puzzled it came after Swiss businesses and the government last week agreed to a humanitarian fund for victims of Nazi persecution.
In a petition blasting government policy, some 200 leading Swiss intellectuals accused the country's leaders of damaging Switzerland's credibility as a neutral state.

"The standing and credibility of Switzerland as a democratic nation are compromised and imperilled," said the petition, signed by leading Swiss personalities including lawyers, doctors, artists, writers, academics and journalists on Wednesday.

The petition was launched in reaction to remarks by outgoing president Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, who dismissed Jewish groups' calls for quick compensation as "extortion and blackmail" last month but later apologised.
